torn/problem: Train a language model, and its loss on a text, averaged over the tokens, comes out at, say, one point three nine. Is that good? On its own, the number is hard to picture.
torn/even: So take a model that is easy to picture. At every step, it spreads its bet evenly over four tokens, a quarter each, like rolling a fair four-sided die.
torn/loss: Whichever token is right got a quarter, so every step's loss is minus ln of a quarter. One over four flips the sign of the log: ln four, about one point three nine.
torn/same: That is our number. A loss of one point three nine per token is exactly as unsure as a fair pick among four.
torn/undo: To get the four back, undo the log: e to the one point three nine is four. That is the perplexity: e to the average loss, L.
torn/k: Spread the bet evenly over two tokens, and the perplexity is two. Over ten, it is ten. Perplexity counts the tokens a model is, in effect, torn between.
torn/q: Only the right token's share counts. Give it a tenth at every step, however the rest is spread, and the loss is ln ten each time: a perplexity of ten.
torn/name: Hence the name. To be perplexed is to be puzzled, torn between ways to go, and the perplexity says how many ways.
torn/history: Frederick Jelinek, Robert Mercer, Lalit Bahl and James Baker, at IBM, proposed it in 1977, to measure how hard a speech recognition task is. The size of the vocabulary, they showed, is not a fair measure; perplexity counts the equally likely choices a task amounts to.
uneven/real: A real model bets unevenly, and differently at every step. Reading four tokens of text, this one gave the right next token a half, then a quarter, a half, and an eighth.
uneven/loss: Each step's loss is minus ln of its share. The eighth costs the most: ln eight, about two point zero eight.
uneven/mean: Average the four losses, and L is about one point two one per token.
uneven/exp: Undo the log: e to the one point two one is about three point three six.
uneven/means: So on average, this model is as torn as a fair pick among about three and a third tokens.
uneven/order: Average first, then undo the log. Undo it on the total loss instead, and you count the choices for the whole text at once: a number that grows the longer the text runs.
scale/one: Perplexity has a floor. A model that gives the right token all of its probability, every time, has a loss of minus ln one at each step: zero. And e to the zero is one: one choice, the right one.
scale/V: A model that has learned nothing spreads its bet evenly over its whole vocabulary of V tokens, so its perplexity is V: with fifty thousand tokens, fifty thousand.
scale/back: Read it backwards, and the loss is the log of the perplexity. A perplexity of twenty is an average loss of ln twenty, about three.
scale/compare: e to the loss climbs whenever the loss does, so the two always rank models the same way. On the same text and vocabulary, a model at twelve beats a model at thirty: it is torn between fewer tokens.
scale/units: To set a loss against a perplexity, put both in the same units first. A loss of two is a perplexity of e squared, about seven point three nine.
